policy: Only models with exact usable ids confirmed by provider documentation enter the default registry; marketing-only names and previews without usable ids wait.
Research previews with real availability (e.g. gpt-5.3-codex-spark on ChatGPT Pro) may enter with status sota for their niche, noted in the description.
No floating aliases (kimi-latest, *-latest). Pin concrete ids so a provider-side model swap cannot bypass this registry.
Every badge names exactly one model. A new badge holder demotes the old one in the same change.
Any change to models bumps version by exactly 1 and refreshes updatedAt.
Deprecated entries keep their replacedBy id for one release so sweeps know what to rewrite, then get deleted.

Building and gating seats are Claude-held: Opus 5 is the default implementer and orchestrator (scope, direction, progress, done-or-not, approve/deny) and Fable 5 holds planning. GPT-5.6 keeps the checking seats (Sol reviews, Terra validates), but Sol and Terra never orchestrate, gate, or carry default implementation, and Luna is for trivial, minimal-risk work only.

routing.intro: As of registry v7 (Claude Opus 5's 2026-07-24 launch), Claude does the building and the gating and GPT-5.6 does the checking. Opus 5 is the default implementer; its launch benchmarks put it ahead of GPT-5.6 Sol on agentic coding (Frontier-Bench v0.1 43.3% vs 34.4%) at lower output cost ($25 vs $30 per million tokens), and it also holds orchestration and gating (scope, choosing direction, whether work progresses, whether it is done). [OpenAI's GPT-5.6 family](https://openai.com/index/gpt-5-6/) keeps the checking seats: Sol for final code review and second opinions, Terra for validation and structured, tool-heavy checking, Luna for trivial cheap passes; maintainer experience is that the 5.6 tiers are strong reviewers but poor gatekeepers.
routing.workflowDefault: Implementation runs on Claude Opus 5: start substantial work there, escalating to Fable 5 only for the most ambitious, longest-horizon builds. Codex checks the work: Sol takes final code review and second opinions on the hardest changes, Terra takes validation, structured checking, and explicitly tool-heavy verification, and Luna is reserved for trivial, minimal-risk work (tiny scoped edits, mechanical transforms, quick lookups, high-volume cheap passes) and research-style gathering; neither Terra nor Luna should carry substantial implementation now that Opus 5 outbenchmarks Sol on agentic coding at lower cost. Orchestration and gating decisions (scope, choosing direction, judging progress, deciding whether something is done, approving or denying gates) also stay on Claude (Opus 5 at medium reasoning effort by default, Fable 5 for planning and for calls where you deliberately want Anthropic's strongest judgment) and never go to GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra, whose findings feed the Claude orchestrator's decision. Agent arrays are sequential fallback chains: a later provider is attempted only when an earlier one is unavailable or fails. An explicitly constructed provider agent is a deliberate choice and can run even when Codex is healthy.
routing.fableGuidance: Fable 5 is not a Codex tier. Anthropic describes it as a model for ambitious, long, complex knowledge and coding work; developers can use `claude-fable-5` through the Claude API at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Anthropic's July 1 redeployment restored access globally on Claude Platform, Claude.ai, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork. For Pro, Max, Team, and select Enterprise plans, Anthropic said Fable 5 would be included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits through July 12, 2026 at 11:59:59 PM PT ([promotion details](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15424964-claude-fable-5-promotional-access)), after which use requires usage credits; standard Enterprise has no included allowance. Anthropic said it would re-enable AWS, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Foundry as quickly as possible, while its current Fable page lists availability through available marketplaces and those cloud platforms, so cloud-provider and account availability should be treated as conditional rather than universal. Its updated safeguards can reroute blocked requests to Opus 4.8 and can false-positive more often during routine coding and debugging. In current Claude applications and Claude Code behavior, that Fable-to-Opus switching is enabled by default, while API customers must opt in and configure the fallback themselves ([default product behavior and API opt-in](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15363606-why-claude-switched-models-in-your-conversation-with-fable-5)). Treat this as current product behavior, not a permanent provider guarantee. Smithers gives Claude the building and orchestration seats outright: Opus 5 holds the implementer and orchestrator defaults (substantial implementation plus gating, scope, direction, progress, done-or-not) and Fable holds planning and the most ambitious builds, with each backing the other up; Fable also remains the non-Codex fallback for Sol-backed review. Codex-backed research, validation, mid-tier, and tool-heavy checking roles fall back to Sonnet instead, not Fable; the cited sources do not establish a general latency comparison. Automatic fallback pools do not silently run Fable in parallel with a healthy Codex path; an explicit Claude/OpenCode workflow may choose it directly. In Claude Code the model id is `claude-fable-5`; the OpenCode configuration uses the provider-qualified id `anthropic/claude-fable-5`.

situations.when: Trivial, minimal-risk work: tiny scoped edits, mechanical changes, quick research and lookups, high-volume cheap passes
situations.escalate: The work is real implementation or carries risk; hand it to Opus 5 (or Terra when you deliberately want a Codex-side build lane)

situations.when: Validation, structured checking, and explicitly tool-heavy verification, or a deliberate Codex-side implementation lane
situations.escalate: The check is genuinely hard, ambiguous, or high-stakes; move review up to Sol. Findings feed the Claude orchestrator, which gates

situations.when: Final code review, second opinions on the hardest changes, and the deepest Codex-side reasoning
situations.escalate: Sol reports findings; it does not gate or carry default implementation. Scope, direction, progress, and done-or-not decisions go to the Claude orchestrator, and human authority goes to a human gate

situations.when: Substantial implementation by default, plus orchestration and gating: scope, choosing direction, judging progress, deciding whether work is done, approving or denying gates (gating runs at medium reasoning effort)
situations.escalate: Escalate to Fable 5 for the most ambitious long-horizon builds or when a call is unusually consequential and you want Anthropic's strongest judgment; use a human gate for decisions that require human authority

situations.when: Planning and design freezes, the most ambitious long-horizon builds, deliberate premium judgment on orchestration calls, or the no-Codex fallback for Sol-backed review
situations.escalate: Use the provider's supported fallback (Opus, then Kimi) or a human gate for decisions that require human authority

situations.when: No usable Codex authentication for the Codex-backed checking seats (research, validation, mid-tier, tool-heavy), or a cheap Claude-native build lane behind Opus 5
situations.escalate: Use the provider's supported fallback (Kimi) or an explicit Claude-native specialist choice

models.name: Claude Fable 5
models.description: Anthropic's Mythos-class model for ambitious, long, complex knowledge and coding work. Developers can use `claude-fable-5` through the Claude API at $10 per million input tokens and $50 per million output tokens. Anthropic's July 1 redeployment restored access on Claude Platform, Claude.ai, Claude Code, and Claude Cowork; the temporary included window for eligible subscription plans runs through July 12, 2026 at 11:59:59 PM PT ([promotion details](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15424964-claude-fable-5-promotional-access)), and cloud-platform availability remains subject to the marketplace, provider, and account. Its updated safeguards may reroute blocked requests to Opus 4.8 and may false-positive during routine coding and debugging. Current Claude applications and Claude Code enable that switching by default, while API customers must opt in and configure it ([default product behavior and API opt-in](https://support.claude.com/en/articles/15363606-why-claude-switched-models-in-your-conversation-with-fable-5)); treat the notice as current product behavior rather than a permanent provider guarantee. Smithers runs planning and design-freeze steps on Fable, escalates unusually consequential orchestration calls to it (Opus 5 holds the orchestrator default), and keeps it as the non-Codex fallback for Sol-backed review and smart work. Claude Code uses `claude-fable-5`; Smithers' OpenCode configuration uses the provider-qualified id `anthropic/claude-fable-5`. See [Anthropic's launch announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-fable-5-mythos-5), [redeployment update](https://www.anthropic.com/news/redeploying-fable-5), and [current Fable availability](https://www.anthropic.com/claude/fable).

models.name: Claude Opus 5
models.description: Anthropic's new Opus flagship and, as of registry v7, both the default Smithers orchestrator and the default implementer: a drop-in replacement for Opus 4.8 at the same $5/$25 per-million-token pricing with a step change in agentic capability. Launch benchmarks: 43.3% on Frontier-Bench v0.1 (Fable 5 33.7%, GPT-5.6 Sol 34.4%; more than double Opus 4.8 at lower cost per task), 30.2% on ARC-AGI-3 (next best 7.8%), 70.6% on OSWorld 2.0 (above Fable 5 at roughly a third of the cost), within 0.5% of Fable 5's peak CursorBench 3.2 score at half the cost per task, and about 1.5x the next-best pass rate on Zapier AutomationBench; Anthropic also reports matching Opus 4.8's max-reasoning quality with ~26% fewer tokens at lower effort. Substantial implementation starts here: it took the seat from GPT-5.6 Terra/Sol because it beats Sol on agentic coding at lower output cost ($25 vs $30 per million tokens), with Fable 5 for the most ambitious builds and Codex Sol/Terra reviewing and validating the output. Orchestration and gating decisions (scope, choosing direction, judging progress, deciding whether work is done, approving or denying gates) also run here, at medium reasoning effort, rather than on GPT-5.6 Sol or Terra, which are strong reviewers but poor gatekeepers. API differences from Opus 4.8: thinking is on by default (omitting `thinking` runs adaptive), disabling thinking is only accepted at effort `high` or below, rate limits draw from a new bucket separate from the combined Opus 4.x pool, and elevated cybersecurity safeguards can return `stop_reason: "refusal"` with Opus 4.8 as the recommended fallback target. See [Anthropic's launch announcement](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-opus-5).

models.name: Claude Opus 4.8
models.description: The previous Opus flagship, superseded by Claude Opus 5 (same pricing, drop-in API surface) as the default Smithers orchestrator and implementer. Retained as a compatibility fallback: it is Anthropic's recommended refusal-fallback target for Fable 5 and Opus 5 safeguard reroutes, and it draws from the combined Opus 4.x rate-limit bucket, which is separate from Opus 5's. This provides useful headroom when Opus 5 quota is tight.

models.name: Claude Sonnet 5
models.description: The newest Sonnet: fast, cheap, 1M context. It is the primary non-Codex fallback for the Codex-backed checking seats (research, validation, mid-tier, tool-heavy) when Codex is unavailable, and the cheap Claude-native build lane behind Opus 5 in the implementation pool; Sol-backed review falls back to Fable instead, and building, orchestration, and planning already run on Claude (Opus 5 and Fable 5).

models.name: Claude Haiku 4.5
models.description: Anthropic's cheapest tier, for high-volume summarization and classification where even Sonnet is overkill.

models.name: GPT-5.6 Sol
models.description: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 flagship and the smartest reviewer in the roster. Use Sol for final code review, second opinions on the hardest or most ambiguous changes, and the deepest Codex-side reasoning. As of registry v7 default implementation runs on Claude Opus 5, which outbenchmarks Sol on agentic coding (Frontier-Bench v0.1 43.3% vs 34.4%) at lower output cost; Sol stays in the smart pool as the Codex-side fallback. Do not use Sol for orchestration or gating (scope, direction, progress, done-or-not): it is a strong reviewer but a poor gatekeeper, and those seats belong to Claude (Opus 5 by default). See [OpenAI's GPT-5.6 release](https://openai.com/index/gpt-5-6/).

models.name: GPT-5.6 Terra
models.description: OpenAI's balanced GPT-5.6 model and the default checking tier: validation, structured checking, and explicitly tool-heavy verification run on Terra, and it remains the deliberate Codex-side build lane when you want a second implementation engine. Default implementation moved to Claude Opus 5 in registry v7. Escalate review to Sol when the check is genuinely hard, ambiguous, or high-stakes. Like Sol, Terra does not orchestrate or gate; its validation findings feed the Claude orchestrator's decision. See [OpenAI's GPT-5.6 release](https://openai.com/index/gpt-5-6/).

models.name: GPT-5.6 Luna
models.description: OpenAI's fastest and most affordable GPT-5.6 tier. In Smithers, Luna handles trivial, minimal-risk work only: tiny scoped edits, mechanical transforms, quick research and lookups, and high-volume cheap passes. Substantial implementation starts on Claude Opus 5 instead (Terra for a deliberate Codex-side lane); escalate rather than letting Luna carry work with real blast radius. See [OpenAI's GPT-5.6 release](https://openai.com/index/gpt-5-6/) and the [GPT-5.6 preview release](https://openai.com/index/previewing-gpt-5-6-sol/).

models.name: GPT-5.5
models.description: The previous OpenAI flagship. Keep it as a compatibility fallback for Codex accounts that do not yet expose GPT-5.6.

models.name: GPT-5.4
models.description: The previous OpenAI flagship, retained for pinned compatibility. New Smithers workflows use the GPT-5.6 Sol/Terra/Luna role split instead.

models.name: GPT-5.4 mini
models.description: OpenAI's prior fast, efficient tier. Retained as the OpenRouter compatibility fallback (openai/gpt-5.4-mini); Codex-native cheap work defaults to GPT-5.6 Luna.

models.name: GPT-5.3-Codex-Spark
models.description: OpenAI's first real-time coding model: 1000+ tokens per second on dedicated Cerebras hardware while staying genuinely capable. Research preview, ChatGPT Pro only. Reach for it when iteration latency matters more than depth.

models.name: Gemini 3.5 Flash
models.description: Google's best price-to-performance model and the best non-Codex fallback for UI work: near-Pro intelligence at Flash speed and cost, 1M context, and it beats Gemini 3.1 Pro on coding and agentic benchmarks while running roughly 4x faster. Smithers can use it for UI work when its provider-specific route is configured; it is not a universal fallback policy.

models.name: Gemini 3.1 Pro
models.description: Google's Pro tier (still preview). Superseded for coding and agentic work by Gemini 3.5 Flash; keep it for long-horizon reasoning where Pro depth wins.

models.name: Gemini 3.1 Flash-Lite
models.description: Frontier-class performance at a fraction of the cost. The floor of the Gemini lineup for bulk, low-stakes calls.

models.name: Kimi K2.7-Code
models.description: Moonshot's most capable coding model: 256k context, roughly 30% fewer reasoning tokens than K2.6, and strong instruction-following in long contexts. Smithers keeps it as a no-Codex implementation fallback; the -highspeed variant trades a little quality for ~180 tok/s.

models.name: Kimi K2.7-Code High-Speed
models.description: The high-throughput K2.7-Code variant, around 180 tokens per second. The open-weights answer to Codex-Spark for latency-sensitive loops.

models.name: Kimi K2.6
models.description: Moonshot's open-source (modified MIT) trillion-parameter MoE flagship: native multimodal, agent swarms up to 300 sub-agents, up to 13 hours of continuous coding. Ties GPT-5.5 on SWE-Bench Pro at roughly 80% lower cost. The strongest model you can self-host.

models.name: Kimi K3
models.description: Moonshot's newest long-context model, served on Kimi-for-Coding: a 1M-token context window with thinking plus image and video input. Its niche is very-long-context coding and mid-run model swaps where a huge window absorbs accumulated state. Exact usable ids: `kimi-code/k3` in the Kimi CLI, `kimi-for-coding/k3` in OpenCode, `moonshotai/kimi-k3` via Cloudflare AI Gateway.
